subject: Cognitive Science
title: Fundamental Attribution Error
description: A quick, practical guide to Fundamental Attribution Error.

hook.text: Someone cuts you off in traffic. "What a jerk!" But when you cut someone off, you had a good reason.

buildup.text: The fundamental attribution error: we blame others' behavior on character but our own on circumstances.

discovery.text: Lee Ross named it in 1977. We overweight personality and underweight the situation others are in.

twist.text: It's weaker in collectivist cultures. East Asian participants consider context more than Westerners do.

climax.text: At work, it creates toxic judgment: a missed deadline becomes a character flaw, not a resource problem.

punchline.text: Before judging character, check the situation.

quiz.question: What is the fundamental attribution error?
options: Blaming others' actions on character, not situation
Always seeing the best in others

details.summary: The fundamental attribution error is the tendency to attribute others' behavior to their character while attributing our own behavior to circumstances. When someone cuts you off in traffic, you think they are reckless; when you do it, you had a good reason. This asymmetry poisons social judgment.
details.whyItMatters: This error fuels interpersonal conflict, prejudice, and unfair blame. It causes people to underestimate how powerfully situations shape behavior and to over-blame individuals.
takeaways: Others' behavior is attributed to character rather than situation
Our own behavior is attributed to circumstances
This asymmetry distorts social judgment systematically

faq.question: Is the fundamental attribution error universal across cultures?
faq.answer: It is strongest in Western, individualist cultures that emphasize personal responsibility. East Asian cultures, which emphasize context and social roles, show the error less strongly. However, some tendency toward dispositional attribution appears across all cultures studied.

faq.question: How can you reduce the fundamental attribution error?
faq.answer: Before judging someone's character, consider situational factors that might explain their behavior. Imagine yourself in their circumstances. Ask what external pressures might be at play. This deliberate perspective-taking reduces but does not eliminate the bias.
